- `setup-modules/shell-env.sh`: Use `{ cmd1; cmd2; } >> file` instead of individual redirects [SC2129] (2 occurrences)
- `setup-modules/core.sh`: Use `{ cmd1; cmd2; } >> file` instead of individual redirects [SC2129] (2 occurrences)

- SC2129: Group multiple redirects to the same file with `{ ...; } >> file`

Ref: quality review issue #2632

title: fix: review-bot-gate passes on rate-limit/quota warnings without actual code review
body:
## Problem

When CodeRabbit or Gemini post rate-limit/quota warning comments on a PR, the `review-bot-gate-helper.sh` reports `PASS` (bots have posted) and the `Wait for AI Review Bots` CI check passes. However, no actual code review occurred — the bots posted error messages, not reviews.

## Observed pattern (2026-03-07)

17 PRs across marcusquinn/aidevops, marcusquinn/aidevops.sh, and marcusquinn/turbostarter-plus all have:
- `review-bot-gate-helper.sh` returning `PASS` (found: coderabbitai gemini-code-assist)
- Formal review count = 0 (no actual reviews)
- CodeRabbit comment: "Rate limit exceeded" 
- Gemini comment: "You have reached your daily quota limit"

The formal review count gate (=0) correctly blocks auto-merge. But the gate check misleadingly reports PASS, which could confuse future pulse logic or human reviewers.

## Root cause

`review-bot-gate-helper.sh` detects bot presence by checking for bot usernames in PR comments. It does not distinguish between rate-limit warnings and actual review comments.

## Proposed fix

In `review-bot-gate-helper.sh`, when a bot comment is found, check whether it contains rate-limit/quota warning patterns (e.g., "Rate limit exceeded", "daily quota limit"). If so, treat it as `WAITING` rather than `PASS` — the bot acknowledged the PR but did not review it.

Alternatively, check for the presence of a CodeRabbit review summary (the `<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: summarize by coderabbit.ai -->` marker combined with actual review content, not just the rate-limit template).

## Impact

Low urgency — the formal review count gate prevents incorrect merges. But the misleading PASS status adds confusion and may cause future pulse logic to incorrectly conclude bots have reviewed when they haven't.

_⚠️ Potential issue_ | _🟠 Major_

<details>
<summary>🧩 Analysis chain</summary>

🌐 Web query:

`GitHub REST API "Get the combined status for a specific reference": does GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/commits/{ref}/status support pagination via `per_page` and `page`, and what is the default page size?`

💡 Result:

Yes. **GET `/repos/{owner}/{repo}/commits/{ref}/status`** supports pagination via the standard query parameters **`per_page`** and **`page`** (with **`per_page` max 100**). The **default page size is `per_page=30`** (and **`page` defaults to `1`**). [1]

**Source(s)**  
[1] https://docs.github.com/en/enterprise-cloud@latest/rest/commits/statuses#parameters-for-get-the-combined-status-for-a-specific-reference

---



</details>

**Add pagination support to the combined-status lookup in the fallback gate check.**

The `gh api` call on line 168 fetches only page 1 of GitHub's combined-status endpoint, which defaults to 30 results per page. Commits with more than 30 statuses will miss matching bot contexts on subsequent pages, causing false negatives. Use `--paginate` with `per_page=100` to fetch all pages, and apply the same fix to `.github/workflows/review-bot-gate.yml`.

The bash example in this section uses `2>/dev/null` to suppress errors from `classify` and `jq` commands. This practice hides valuable debugging information, such as API failures, malformed JSON, or missing dependencies, which goes against the repository's general rules. The `||` construct already handles command failures gracefully. Removing `2>/dev/null` will make this example script more robust and easier to debug without changing its behavior on success.

```markdown
DECOMPOSE_HELPER="$HOME/.aidevops/agents/scripts/task-decompose-helper.sh"

# Only run if the helper exists (t1408.1 must be merged)
if [[ -x "$DECOMPOSE_HELPER" && -n "$TASK_ID" ]]; then
  # Check if subtasks already exist
  EXISTING=$(/bin/bash "$DECOMPOSE_HELPER" classify --task-id "$TASK_ID" --repo-path "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)" --quiet) || EXISTING=""
  EXISTING_KIND=$(echo "$EXISTING" | jq -r '.kind // "atomic"' || echo "atomic")

  if [[ "$EXISTING_KIND" == "composite" ]]; then
    EXISTING_SUBS=$(echo "$EXISTING" | jq -r '.existing_subtasks // empty' || echo "")
    if [[ -n "$EXISTING_SUBS" && "$EXISTING_SUBS" != "[]" ]]; then
      # Subtasks already exist — skip decomposition
      echo "[t1408.2] Task $TASK_ID already has subtasks — proceeding with implementation"
    fi
  fi

  # If no existing subtasks, classify the task description
  if [[ -z "$EXISTING_SUBS" || "$EXISTING_SUBS" == "[]" ]]; then
    CLASSIFY=$(/bin/bash "$DECOMPOSE_HELPER" classify --task "$TASK_DESC" --task-id "$TASK_ID" --repo-path "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)" --quiet) || CLASSIFY=""
    TASK_KIND=$(echo "$CLASSIFY" | jq -r '.kind // "atomic"' || echo "atomic")
  fi
fi
```

title: t1413: Add memory consolidation phase (cross-memory insight generation)
body:
## Summary

Add a memory consolidation phase to `memory-audit-pulse.sh` that uses a cheap LLM call (haiku-tier, ~$0.001/call) to scan unconsolidated memories, discover cross-cutting connections, and store synthesized insights as new `derives` relations in the existing `learning_relations` table.

## Problem

The existing memory system is maintenance-oriented: dedup removes noise, prune removes staleness, graduate promotes value. But no phase actively **connects** memories to discover patterns. A user who stores "CORS fix: add nginx headers" and later stores "nginx proxy_pass config for API" has two related memories that are never linked.

## Solution

New `phase_consolidate()` in `memory-audit-pulse.sh` (Phase 3.5) that:
1. Queries unconsolidated memories (not yet in any consolidation)
2. Sends batch to `ai-research-helper.sh` (haiku tier) for pattern detection
3. Stores connections as `derives` relations in `learning_relations`
4. Records insights in new `memory_consolidations` table

## Inspired by

Google's [always-on-memory-agent](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/generative-ai/tree/main/gemini/agents/always-on-memory-agent) consolidation loop — adapted to aidevops's batch-oriented architecture (runs in audit pulse, not as a daemon).

## Brief

![security-medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/security-medium-priority.svg) ![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

A critical vulnerability exists in the `cmd_classify_deep` function within `prompt-guard-helper.sh`. It implements a fail-open policy where if the Tier 2 LLM classifier (`content-classifier-helper.sh`) fails (e.g., due to execution errors, API timeouts, or large content), the system incorrectly treats the content as `CLEAN` and returns 0. This allows potentially malicious content to bypass security controls. The `tier2_exit` code is captured but not checked, and `2>/dev/null` currently suppresses critical errors, hiding the underlying cause of classifier failures. This behavior undermines the security benefits of the multi-tier architecture.

```shell
local tier2_result
	local tier2_exit=0
	if [[ -n "$repo" && -n "$author" ]]; then
		tier2_result=$("$classifier" classify-if-external "$repo" "$author" "$content") || tier2_exit=$?
	else
		tier2_result=$("$classifier" classify "$content") || tier2_exit=$?
	fi

	local tier2_class
	tier2_class=$(printf '%s' "$tier2_result" | cut -d'|' -f1)

	if [[ "$tier2_class" == "MALICIOUS" || "$tier2_class" == "SUSPICIOUS" ]]; then
		_pg_log_warn "Tier 2 classification: ${tier2_result}"
		if [[ -n "$tier1_results" ]]; then
			_pg_print_findings "$tier1_results"
		fi
		echo "TIER2_${tier2_class}|${tier2_result}"
		return 1
	fi

	# Fail securely: if Tier 2 failed or returned UNKNOWN, do not return CLEAN
	if [[ "$tier2_exit" -ne 0 || "$tier2_class" == "UNKNOWN" || -z "$tier2_class" ]]; then
		_pg_log_error "Tier 2 classification failed or returned UNKNOWN (exit ${tier2_exit}): ${tier2_result}"
		if [[ -n "$tier1_results" ]]; then
			_pg_print_findings "$tier1_results"
			echo "TIER1_WARN_T2_FAIL"
			return 1
		fi
		echo "ERROR_T2_FAIL|${tier2_result}"
		return 2
	fi

	# Both tiers agree it's clean

		local max_severity
		max_severity=$(_pg_num_to_severity "$(_pg_max_severity "$tier1_results")")
		_pg_log_info "Tier 1: ${max_severity} findings, Tier 2: SAFE — allowing"
```

The `generate_sandbox_env` function constructs shell `export` statements by embedding variables like `sandbox_dir`, `REAL_HOME`, and `GH_TOKEN` directly into single-quoted strings without proper escaping. If any of these variables contain a single quote character (`'`), it will terminate the intended string and allow for arbitrary command injection when the generated environment lines are subsequently executed (e.g., when they are echoed into a wrapper script and run).
```shell
generate_sandbox_env() {
	local sandbox_dir="$1"

	if [[ -z "$sandbox_dir" || ! -d "$sandbox_dir" ]]; then
		echo "ERROR: valid sandbox_dir required" >&2
		return 1
	fi

	# Core: override HOME
	printf "export HOME=%q\n" "${sandbox_dir}"

	# Preserve REAL_HOME so scripts that need the actual home can find it
	# (e.g., for reading repos.json, which is a framework config not a credential)
	printf "export REAL_HOME=%q\n" "${REAL_HOME}"

	# GH_TOKEN: if set in the current environment, pass it through.
	# This is the primary auth mechanism for workers (env var, not filesystem).
	# The dispatch script is responsible for setting GH_TOKEN before calling this.
	if [[ -n "${GH_TOKEN:-}" ]]; then
		printf "export GH_TOKEN=%q\n" "${GH_TOKEN}"
	fi

	# XDG overrides to keep tool state inside the sandbox
	printf "export XDG_CONFIG_HOME=%q\n" "${sandbox_dir}/.config"
	printf "export XDG_DATA_HOME=%q\n" "${sandbox_dir}/.local/share"
	printf "export XDG_CACHE_HOME=%q\n" "${sandbox_dir}/.cache"

	# npm config to use sandbox directory
	printf "export npm_config_cache=%q\n" "${sandbox_dir}/.npm"

	# Prevent tools from reading the real home's dotfiles
	printf "export GNUPGHOME=%q\n" "${sandbox_dir}/.gnupg"

	# Signal to the worker that it's sandboxed (for conditional logic)
	echo "export AIDEVOPS_SANDBOXED=true"
	printf "export AIDEVOPS_SANDBOX_DIR=%q\n" "${sandbox_dir}"

	return 0
}
```

Using `--argjson` also makes it trivial to support floating-point numbers, not just integers.

```suggestion
			print_error "Invalid number value: $value"
			return 1
		fi
		jq --argjson v "$value" "$jq_path = \$v" "$SETTINGS_FILE" >"$tmp_file"
		;;
```

This pattern of suppressing stderr with `2>/dev/null` and then re-running the command on failure is inefficient and violates the repository style guide (line 50), which discourages blanket stderr suppression. This also requires proper temp file cleanup with a `trap` as per the style guide (line 33).

```suggestion
	local stderr_file
	stderr_file=$(mktemp)
	# Per t196, ensure we don't clobber existing RETURN traps.
	local prev_return_trap
	prev_return_trap=$(trap -p RETURN)
	trap 'rm -f "$stderr_file"; eval "${prev_return_trap:-}"' RETURN

	claim_output=$("$claim_script" "${claim_args[@]}" 2> "$stderr_file") || claim_rc=$?

	# Exit code 1 = hard error
	if [[ $claim_rc -eq 1 ]]; then
		log_error "claim-task-id.sh failed. Stderr:"
		# Indent stderr for readability in logs
		sed 's/^/    /' < "$stderr_file" >&2
		return 1
	fi
```

### MEDIUM: gemini (gemini-code-assist[bot])
**File**: `.agents/scripts/response-scoring-helper.sh:402`
![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

The SQL query uses multiple correlated subqueries to fetch per-criterion scores. This can be inefficient as it may execute a subquery for each row. A more performant approach is to use a `LEFT JOIN` on the `scores` table and then use conditional aggregation (`MAX(CASE ...)` with `GROUP BY`) to pivot the scores into columns. This will retrieve all the data in a single, more efficient query.

```suggestion
result=$(sqlite3 -separator '|' "$SCORING_DB" "
        SELECT r.model_id, p.category, p.difficulty,
               ${WEIGHTED_AVG_SQL} as weighted_avg,
               r.token_count, r.cost_estimate,
               MAX(CASE WHEN s.criterion = 'correctness' THEN s.score END) as corr,
               MAX(CASE WHEN s.criterion = 'completeness' THEN s.score END) as comp,
               MAX(CASE WHEN s.criterion = 'code_quality' THEN s.score END) as cq,
               MAX(CASE WHEN s.criterion = 'clarity' THEN s.score END) as clar
        FROM responses r
        JOIN prompts p ON r.prompt_id = p.prompt_id
        LEFT JOIN scores s ON r.response_id = s.response_id
        WHERE r.response_id = ${response_id}
        GROUP BY r.response_id;
    ")
```

While I understand the goal of cleaning up the SonarCloud report by excluding these code smell rules for the large existing shell script codebase, applying these exclusions globally to `**/*.sh` has significant long-term maintainability implications. It will prevent SonarCloud from flagging these issues in any new or modified shell scripts, potentially allowing new technical debt to accumulate.

Specifically, disabling these two rules globally seems particularly risky:

*   **`S1481` (Unused variables):** This rule is very effective at catching typos in variable names and identifying dead code. Disabling it could mask genuine bugs in the future.
*   **`S1192` (String literals):** While the rationale mentions color codes, this rule also helps enforce the use of constants for other magic strings (e.g., URLs, key names, common messages), which is crucial for maintainability in a large project.

Have you considered alternative approaches?

1.  **Bulk change in SonarCloud UI:** You can mark all existing 260 issues as `Won't Fix`. This acknowledges the technical debt on the current code but keeps the rules active for new code, which is generally the recommended practice.
2.  **More targeted exclusions:** If possible, could the `resourceKey` be scoped to directories containing the older scripts that you don't plan to refactor?

If the decision is to proceed with global exclusions, it would be good to document this as a conscious acceptance of technical debt and perhaps create a follow-up task to periodically review and tighten these rules.

title: fix: CodeRabbit daily quota exhausted — 15+ PRs blocked from formal review
body:
## Problem

CodeRabbit's daily review quota is exhausted, blocking all open PRs from receiving formal reviews. This prevents the merge pipeline from advancing since the mandatory review-count gate requires at least 1 formal review before merging.

**Evidence:** PR #3725 has 7 comments but 0 formal reviews. CodeRabbit posted:
> You have reached your daily quota limit. Please wait up to 24 hours and I will start processing your requests again!

**Affected PRs (15 in aidevops alone):** #3725, #3720, #3628, #3620, #3618, #3590, #3579, #3545, #3542, #3394, #3324, #3304, #3146, #3106, #3098

**Root cause:** The pulse is creating too many PRs per day, exhausting CodeRabbit's hourly/daily review quota. With 15+ open PRs all created in a short window, the quota is hit before all PRs get reviewed.

## Impact

- All 15 aidevops PRs are blocked from merging
- The merge pipeline is stalled
- Quality-debt PRs accumulate without review

## Proposed fixes

1. **Rate-limit PR creation in the pulse** — add a daily cap on new PRs created per repo (e.g., max 5/day) to stay within CodeRabbit's quota
2. **Batch quality-debt PRs** — instead of one PR per quality-debt issue, batch related issues into a single PR to reduce PR volume
3. **Upgrade CodeRabbit plan** if the current plan's quota is insufficient for the PR volume
4. **Add quota-aware dispatch** — check CodeRabbit quota status before dispatching workers that will create PRs

## Workaround

Wait 24 hours for quota to reset, then the next pulse cycle will find reviews and merge the backlog.

The `scan_content` function implements a three-layer scanning pipeline where Layer 1 is a keyword pre-filter (`_cs_prefilter`) that skips the entire scan if no suspicious keywords are found. However, this pre-filter runs on the original, un-normalized content. Layer 2 (NFKC normalization) is intended to catch Unicode bypasses (like mathematical-script or fullwidth characters), but it is only executed if the pre-filter matches a keyword. An attacker can use Unicode characters (e.g., `𝐈𝐠𝐧𝐨𝐫𝐞` instead of `Ignore`) to bypass the pre-filter entirely, causing the script to return `CLEAN` without ever performing normalization or the full regex scan. This completely defeats the purpose of the normalization layer.

The `_cs_prefilter` function uses a case-insensitive substring check to identify suspicious keywords. title: t1419: Standalone worker watchdog — auto-detect and kill hung/idle workers
body:
## Problem

When multiple headless workers are dispatched (manually or via pulse), workers that crash, hang, or enter OpenCode's idle-state bug are not automatically detected or cleaned up. The existing watchdog mechanisms in `pulse-wrapper.sh` only monitor the pulse process itself — not independently dispatched workers.

**Observed failure (2026-03-08):** 6 workers dispatched manually, 4 crashed/hung within 5 minutes (thundering herd on MCP cold boot), 1 buffered (API rate limiting), 1 kept working. Required manual consolidation to 1 worker. A second interactive session later hung indefinitely.

## Root Cause

Three failure modes, one systemic gap:

1. **Early crashes (thundering herd):** 6 simultaneous cold boots exhaust RAM (each worker spawns Node.js + language servers + MCP connections). No capacity enforcement for manual dispatch.
2. **Buffering:** Concurrent API calls from same key cause rate-limiting queuing.
3. **Hangs (idle-state bug):** OpenCode enters file-watcher idle state after completing but never exits. Pulse watchdog only covers pulse process, not workers.

## Solution

Create `worker-watchdog.sh` — a standalone launchd service that monitors ALL headless `opencode run` processes:

1. **Extract shared functions** from `pulse-wrapper.sh` into `worker-lifecycle-common.sh` (process age, CPU tree, kill tree)
2. **Create `worker-watchdog.sh`** (~200 lines):
   - Scans all `opencode run` headless processes
   - Three detection signals: CPU idle (5min), progress stall (10min), runtime ceiling (3h)
   - On kill: comment on associated issue, relabel to `status:available`
   - Capacity warnings when total workers exceed MAX_WORKERS
3. **Launchd plist** `sh.aidevops.worker-watchdog.plist` (every 60s, independent of pulse)
4. **Stagger protection** guidance for manual multi-worker dispatch

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `worker-watchdog.sh` detects and kills idle workers within 5 minutes
- [ ] `worker-watchdog.sh` detects and kills stalled workers within 10 minutes

title: refactor: standardize on pre-increment ((++var)) across all shell scripts
body:
## Summary

Standardize all shell scripts to use pre-increment `((++var))` instead of post-increment `((var++))` to prevent `set -e` early exit bugs.

## Background

PR #70 fixed a critical bug in `generate-opencode-commands.sh` where `((command_count++))` with `set -e` caused the script to exit when `command_count=0` (post-increment returns the old value, which is 0/falsy, triggering `set -e` exit). CodeRabbit's review (PR #70, issue #3793) identified that this same unsafe pattern exists in 15+ other scripts.

## Scope

Audit found **113 unsafe post-increment patterns** across **50+ scripts** (excluding `for ((...))` loops and patterns already guarded with `|| true`).

Key affected scripts (non-exhaustive):
- `agent-sources-helper.sh` (7 instances)
- `linters-local.sh` (4 instances)
- `pre-commit-hook.sh` (10 instances)
- `beads-sync-helper.sh` (3 instances)
- `site-crawler-helper.sh` (6 instances)
- `aidevops.sh` (12 instances)
- `mcp-register-claude.sh` (6 instances)
- `postflight-check.sh` (2 instances)
- `todo-ready.sh` (6 instances)

## Fix

For each instance, change `((var++))` to `((++var))`. This is safe because:
- Pre-increment returns the new value (always > 0 after first increment)
- Semantically equivalent when the return value isn't used (which is the case for all standalone increment statements)
- `for ((...))` loop increments are NOT affected (they don't trigger `set -e`)

## Notes

- Scripts already using `|| true` guard are safe but should still be migrated for consistency
- Archived scripts (`archived/`) can be skipped
- This was identified as a medium finding in PR #70 review by CodeRabbit

Closes #3793 (partially — the command generator duplication was addressed in a separate PR)

title: t1524: aidevops update deploys CLI but not agents — stale agent detection gap
body:
## Bug Report

### Description

When `aidevops update` is run inside OpenCode (or any environment where `setup.sh --non-interactive` fails silently), the git repo and CLI update successfully but agents at `~/.aidevops/agents/` are not redeployed. The auto-update poller then sees repo=remote and declares "up to date" forever, creating a permanent mismatch.

### Observed Behaviour

- CLI/repo VERSION: 2.170.0
- Deployed agents VERSION: 2.158.0 (12 releases behind)
- `aidevops status` reports "Up to date" (checks repo, not deployed agents)
- Auto-update log: `Already up to date (v2.170.0)` every 10 minutes — never detects stale agents
- User saw changelog and success message during update, but agents were not deployed

### Root Cause (confirmed via code review)

**Two gaps in the update pipeline:**

**1. `cmd_update()` in `aidevops.sh` (line ~744) — no exit code check on setup.sh**

```bash
# Line 724: success message printed BEFORE setup.sh runs
print_success "Updated to version $new_version"
# ...changelog printed...
# Line 744: setup.sh runs, but failure is not caught
bash "$INSTALL_DIR/setup.sh" --non-interactive
# Line 749: cleanup runs regardless
git checkout -- . 2>/dev/null || true
```

The success message and changelog are printed based on `git pull` succeeding, not on agent deployment completing. If `setup.sh` fails, the user sees a false "updated successfully" report.

**2. `cmd_check()` in `auto-update-helper.sh` (line ~903) — no stale-agent detection**

```bash
current=$(get_local_version)   # reads $INSTALL_DIR/VERSION (repo)
remote=$(get_remote_version)   # reads GitHub API
if [[ "$current" == "$remote" ]]; then
    log_info "Already up to date (v$current)"  # never checks deployed agents
    return 0
fi
```

The poller compares repo VERSION vs GitHub API. Once the repo is current, it never checks if `~/.aidevops/agents/VERSION` matches. A failed `setup.sh` creates a permanent mismatch the poller cannot self-heal.

**Note:** `cmd_update()` DOES have stale-agent detection on the "already up to date" path (lines 686-695), so running `aidevops update` a *second* time catches the mismatch. But the user has no reason to re-run an update that reported success.

### Proposed Fix

1. **`cmd_update()` — verify deployment after setup.sh:**
   - Check `setup.sh` exit code
   - After setup.sh runs, compare `$INSTALL_DIR/VERSION` with `~/.aidevops/agents/VERSION`
   - If mismatch, warn the user: "Agent deployment may have failed. Run `./setup.sh` manually from `~/Git/aidevops/`"

2. **`cmd_check()` — add stale-agent detection to the "up to date" path:**
   - After confirming repo=remote, check `~/.aidevops/agents/VERSION`
   - If stale, re-run `setup.sh --non-interactive`
   - Log: "Deployed agents stale ($deployed), re-deploying..."

3. **Move success message after deployment verification** (optional improvement)

### Environment

- Platform: Linux (Ubuntu)
- RAM: 15GB
- aidevops: 2.170.0 (CLI), 2.158.0 (agents)
- Trigger: `aidevops update` run inside OpenCode session

### Files to Modify

- `aidevops.sh`: `cmd_update()` (~line 724-750)
- `.agents/scripts/auto-update-helper.sh`: `cmd_check()` (~line 866-910)

title: ShellCheck memory explosion: circular source chain + stale wrapper missing RSS watchdog
body:
## Bug Report

### Description

ShellCheck processes spawned by the bash-language-server reach 7-14 GB RSS, consuming nearly all RAM on a 15GB machine. The process guard kills them but they regrow within seconds.

### Observed Behaviour

From `~/.aidevops/logs/memory-pressure.log`:

| Timestamp | ShellCheck RSS | Total aidevops RSS |
|-----------|---------------|-------------------|
| Mar 8 13:02 | 7,583 MB | 9,115 MB |
| Mar 9 12:25 | 2,922 MB | — |
| Mar 9 12:27 | 6,653 + 4,343 + 3,584 MB | **14,687 MB** |
| Mar 9 12:28 | **13,974 MB** | 14,220 MB |

Machine: 15 GB RAM, Linux (Ubuntu), ShellCheck 0.11.0

### Root Cause (confirmed via code review + reproduction)

**Three factors combine:**

**1. Circular source chain between `shared-constants.sh` and `config-helper.sh`**

```
shared-constants.sh:1420 → source "$_CONFIG_HELPER"   (config-helper.sh)
config-helper.sh:37      → source "${_CONFIG_HELPER_DIR}/shared-constants.sh"
```

Runtime-safe (include guard `_SHARED_CONSTANTS_LOADED` at shared-constants.sh:14). But ShellCheck is a static analyzer — it doesn't execute guards. When run with `--external-sources` + `--source-path=<scripts-dir>`, ShellCheck follows the cycle infinitely, consuming exponential memory.

Reproduction:
```bash
# Hangs forever, eating all RAM:
shellcheck --external-sources --source-path=~/.aidevops/agents/scripts/ --format=json1 --shell=bash - <<< '#!/bin/bash
source "${SCRIPT_DIR}/shared-constants.sh"'

# Safe (wrapper strips --external-sources):
shellcheck --source-path=~/.aidevops/agents/scripts/ --format=json1 --shell=bash - <<< '#!/bin/bash
source "${SCRIPT_DIR}/shared-constants.sh"'
# → SC1091 "Not following" — instant, no memory issue
```

**2. bash-language-server hardcodes `--external-sources`** (index.js:82)

The bash-language-server always passes `--external-sources` to ShellCheck. The `shellcheck-wrapper.sh` strips this flag. However, the wrapper may be bypassed:

The language server first reads `SHELLCHECK_PATH` from env (→ wrapper), then calls `connection.workspace.getConfiguration('bashIde')` (server.js:167). If the LSP client (OpenCode) returns `{}` for this section, `ConfigSchema.parse({})` fills Zod defaults including `shellcheckPath: 'shellcheck'` (config.js:38) — overriding the wrapper with the real binary.

**3. Deployed wrapper (v2.158.0) has no RSS watchdog**

The user's agents are stuck at v2.158.0 (see #3980). The v2.158.0 wrapper relies solely on `ulimit -v` for memory limiting. **Confirmed: `ulimit -v` does NOT prevent the explosion on this Linux system** (overcommit_memory=0, ShellCheck survived 15s timeout with 512MB ulimit). The v2.170.0 wrapper has a background RSS watchdog that polls every 2 seconds and kills at 1GB — but it's not deployed.

### Impact

- Near-total RAM exhaustion (14.7 GB / 15 GB)
- Swap thrashing (1.7 GB swap used after events)
- Process guard kills restore stability within ~1 minute, but the cycle repeats
- Affects any OpenCode session where the bash-language-server analyzes scripts that source `shared-constants.sh`

### Proposed Fix (layered)

**Layer 1: Break the circular source chain (root cause)**

Add ShellCheck-visible cycle guard in `config-helper.sh`:

```bash
# Replace line 36-37:
if [[ -z "${_SHARED_CONSTANTS_LOADED:-}" ]]; then
    # shellcheck source=/dev/null
    source "${_CONFIG_HELPER_DIR}/shared-constants.sh" 2>/dev/null || true
fi
```

`# shellcheck source=/dev/null` tells ShellCheck to NOT follow this specific source, breaking the cycle at the static analysis level without affecting runtime behaviour.

**Layer 2: Prevent LSP config override (defense-in-depth)**

Either:
- a) Set `SHELLCHECK_ARGUMENTS` env var to include something that identifies the wrapper is expected (fragile)
- b) Patch the shellcheck-wrapper.sh to also install itself at a PATH location that the default `shellcheck` resolves to (e.g., symlink)
- c) File upstream issue against bash-language-server to not override env-based config with schema defaults

**Layer 3: Agent update (already tracked in #3980)**

Updating agents to v2.170.0 deploys the RSS watchdog wrapper — the most robust mitigation. This is already tracked.

### Files to Modify

- `.agents/scripts/config-helper.sh:36-37` — add `# shellcheck source=/dev/null`
- Optionally: `.agents/scripts/shared-constants.sh:1419` — add `# shellcheck source=/dev/null` (belt and braces)

### Related

- #3980 — Agent update stale (blocks Layer 3 fix)
- GH#2915 — Original ShellCheck memory explosion incident
- PR#2918, PR#2937 — Previous fixes for source-path recursion

### Environment

- Platform: Linux (Ubuntu)
- RAM: 15 GB
- ShellCheck: 0.11.0
- Agents: v2.158.0 (stale, should be v2.170.0)
- bash-language-server: bundled with OpenCode

## Unactioned Review Feedback

**Source PR**: #3960
**File**: `.agents/scripts/loop-common.sh`
**Reviewers**: gemini, human

---

### MEDIUM: gemini (gemini-code-assist[bot])
**File**: `.agents/scripts/loop-common.sh:213`
![security-medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/security-medium-priority.svg) ![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

The fix for JQ injection in `loop_set_state` is incomplete. While the `$value` is now safely handled using `--arg`, the `$key` variable is still interpolated directly into the JQ filter string. If the key is derived from untrusted input (e.g., a dynamic field name from a task or user metadata), an attacker could inject arbitrary JQ filters to manipulate the state file, potentially leading to logic bypasses or data corruption.

To remediate this, avoid direct interpolation of the key. If the key is a simple identifier, you can use the `.[$key]` syntax. For nested paths, consider using JQ's `setpath` function with the path components passed as an array.

<details>
<summary>References</summary>

1. In shell scripts, use `jq --arg` for strings and `--argjson` for other JSON types (like numbers) to safely pass variables into a `jq` filter. This avoids syntax errors if the variables contain special characters.
</details>

[View comment](https://github.com/marcusquinn/aidevops/pull/3960#discussion_r2903222835)
---

### MEDIUM: gemini (gemini-code-assist[bot])
**File**: `.agents/scripts/loop-common.sh:1014`
![security-medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/security-medium-priority.svg) ![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

The `$completion_promise` variable is interpolated directly into a regular expression for `grep -qE`. This introduces a regex injection vulnerability. If the promise string contains regex metacharacters (e.g., `.*`, `|`, `^`), it could lead to unintended matches, allowing an untrusted LLM output to bypass the completion check by providing a string that matches the manipulated regex instead of the specific expected promise.

To remediate this, ensure the promise string is escaped before being used in the regex, or use a fixed-string match if possible while still allowing for the desired whitespace tolerance.

[View comment](https://github.com/marcusquinn/aidevops/pull/3960#discussion_r2903222839)
---

### MEDIUM: gemini (gemini-code-assist[bot])
**File**: `.agents/scripts/loop-common.sh:1100`
![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

While this consolidation is a great performance improvement, suppressing stderr with `2>/dev/null` can hide important errors if `jq` fails (e.g., if `$LOOP_STATE_FILE` is missing or malformed). This makes debugging more difficult. It's better to remove the redirection to allow potential errors to be visible.

```suggestion

```

<details>
<summary>References</summary>

1. Avoid using '2>/dev/null' for blanket suppression of command errors in shell scripts to ensure that authentication, syntax, or system issues remain visible for debugging.
</details>

[View comment](https://github.com/marcusquinn/aidevops/pull/3960#discussion_r2903222841)
---

### MEDIUM: gemini (gemini-code-assist[bot])
**File**: `.agents/scripts/loop-common.sh:1113`
![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

Suppressing stderr for the `find` command can hide issues, for example if `$LOOP_RECEIPTS_DIR` does not exist. Removing `2>/dev/null` would make such errors visible and aid in debugging.

```suggestion
    receipt_count=$(find "$LOOP_RECEIPTS_DIR" -name "*.json" -type f | grep -c . || echo "0")
```

<details>
<summary>References</summary>

1. Avoid using '2>/dev/null' for blanket suppression of command errors in shell scripts to ensure that authentication, syntax, or system issues remain visible for debugging.
</details>

[View comment](https://github.com/marcusquinn/aidevops/pull/3960#discussion_r2903222851)
---

### MEDIUM: human (marcusquinn)
**File**: `.agents/scripts/loop-common.sh:213`
Valid finding — fixed. All callers currently pass hardcoded key literals (e.g., `.iteration`, `.active`), so the risk was theoretical, but the function signature accepts arbitrary $1 so a future caller could introduce injection. Now using `--arg k` with `.[\]` syntax for all branches (integer via `--argjson`, boolean via `--argjson`, null, and string via `--arg`). The leading dot is stripped from the key path before passing to `--arg`.

[View comment](https://github.com/marcusquinn/aidevops/pull/3960#discussion_r2903358235)
---

### MEDIUM: human (marcusquinn)
**File**: `.agents/scripts/loop-common.sh:1014`
Valid finding — fixed. Replaced `grep -qE` with regex-interpolated promise with a two-step approach: (1) `grep -qF "<promise>"` for a fast fixed-string pre-check, (2) `sed` extraction of the content between `<promise>...</promise>` tags with whitespace trimming, (3) literal string comparison via `[[ "\$extracted_promise" == "\$completion_promise" ]]`. This eliminates the regex injection vector while preserving whitespace tolerance.

[View comment](https://github.com/marcusquinn/aidevops/pull/3960#discussion_r2903358444)
---

### MEDIUM: human (marcusquinn)
**File**: `.agents/scripts/loop-common.sh:1100`
Intentional — not changing. The `2>/dev/null` here is a deliberate design choice for a status display function. The guard `[[ ! -f "$LOOP_STATE_FILE" ]]` on line 1080 already handles the missing-file case with a clean "No active loop" message. The stderr suppression prevents noisy jq parse errors from corrupting the formatted status output when the state file is transiently malformed (e.g., mid-write from another process). In a status display context, a graceful degradation (empty fields) is preferable to stderr noise that breaks the output format.

[View comment](https://github.com/marcusquinn/aidevops/pull/3960#discussion_r2903358701)
---

**File**: `.agents/scripts/loop-common.sh:1113`
Intentional — not changing. `$LOOP_RECEIPTS_DIR` may not exist yet when no receipts have been created (the directory is created on first receipt). The `2>/dev/null` suppresses the expected "No such file or directory" from `find`, and the `|| echo "0"` fallback ensures a clean count of 0. This is a status display function — surfacing an expected filesystem error would add noise without actionable information.

title: t1424: Zero-config localdev — auto-register projects and `localdev run` wrapper
body:
## Context

Two convenience gaps vs portless that make our localdev stack feel manual:

1. **Manual registration** — user must run `localdev add myapp` before `https://myapp.local` works. portless infers the project name from `package.json`/git automatically.

2. **Manual port passing** — after registration, user must know the assigned port and pass it: `PORT=3100 npm run dev`. portless wraps the command and injects the port automatically.

## What

### `localdev run` command

```bash
# In ~/Git/myapp/ (not yet registered)
localdev run npm run dev
# -> Auto-registers myapp (cert, Traefik route, /etc/hosts, port 3100)
# -> Sets PORT=3100 HOST=0.0.0.0
# -> Runs: npm run dev
# -> https://myapp.local just works

# In a worktree ~/Git/myapp-bugfix-fix-thing/
localdev run npm run dev
# -> Auto-detects worktree, creates branch subdomain
# -> Sets PORT=3101
# -> Runs: npm run dev
# -> https://fix-thing.myapp.local just works
```

### Auto-register on worktree creation

When `localdev_auto_branch()` in `worktree-helper.sh` detects an unregistered project, auto-run `localdev add` before creating the branch route. No manual step needed.

## Subtasks

- [ ] t1424.1 Auto-register in `localdev_auto_branch()` — detect unregistered project, infer name from repo basename or `package.json`, run `localdev add` automatically
- [ ] t1424.2 `localdev run <command>` — wrapper that auto-registers if needed, resolves the correct port (main or branch), sets PORT/HOST env vars, execs the command. Process management: foreground by default, SIGINT/SIGTERM passthrough
- [ ] t1424.3 Update `local-hosting.md` — document `localdev run` as the primary workflow, update Quick Reference and examples

## Why

Closes the zero-config convenience gap with portless without adopting a 3-week-old experimental dependency. Users get `localdev run npm run dev` → named HTTPS URL, same as portless's `portless run npm run dev` but with production-parity Traefik routing, real TLS on port 443, and Docker container support.

Triggered by PR #3996 review discussion.
